abstract: New species evolve in a complex and non-linear fashion, resulting in situations where genomic and phenotypic variation between diverging lineages become decoupled. For example, natural selection acting on traits commonly used to diagnose species can instead drive trait variation to disagree with genomic evidence for species boundaries, challenging systematists aiming to delimit species. In this study, we combine phylogenetic, population genomic, and coalescent-based gene flow analyses to test whether convergence of a signaling trait has a shared genomic basis and to evaluate the evidence for unrecognized species level diversity in the Anolis distichus species group, a polytypic clade of lizards spanning the island of Hispaniola and the Bahamas in which diversity of a sex-linked signaling trait conflicts with genetic evidence for species boundaries. Comparing evolutionary histories of autosomes, sex chromosomes, and mitochondrial DNA, we find that the entire spectrum of signaling trait variation is present in four major geographic clades of the A. distichus species group and recover support for the independent evolution of this convergent signal. By quantifying isolation-by-distance and inferring migration across all contact zones on Hispaniola, we find evidence for lineages spanning the entire speciation continuum---from interbreeding populations to lineages exhibiting signatures of strong reproductive isolation. Together, our study highlights how phenotypic and genomic divergence may decouple during speciation, and provides a robust framework for gene flow-informed taxonomic revisions of the A. distichus species group.
